history.heading: Kingdom of Dahomey
paragraphs: Several kingdoms developed in present-day Benin, including Allada, Porto-Novo and, most powerfully, Dahomey, founded in the early 17th century with its capital at Abomey. Dahomey had a centralised administration and an army that included a famous corps of female soldiers, known to Europeans as the Dahomey Amazons.

Dahomey became a major participant in the Atlantic slave trade, selling captives from wars to European traders at Ouidah, a port through which over a million Africans were shipped. The Royal Palaces of Abomey are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

history.heading: French colony
paragraphs: France conquered Dahomey in 1892–94 after wars against King Béhanzin, and the territory became a colony within French West Africa. Dahomey developed a well-educated elite, earning it the nickname "Latin Quarter of Africa".

history.heading: Independence and democracy
paragraphs: Dahomey became independent on 1 August 1960. A series of coups followed until Mathieu Kérékou took power in 1972 and established a Marxist-Leninist state, renaming the country Benin in 1975.

Economic crisis led to a pioneering national conference in 1990, which ended the one-party state and inspired democratic transitions across Africa. Benin became known as one of the continent's most stable democracies, though concerns about democratic backsliding have grown since the late 2010s.

culture.heading: Birthplace of Vodun
paragraphs: Benin is considered the birthplace of Vodun (Voodoo), a religion whose influence spread to Haiti, Brazil and the Americas through the slave trade. Vodun is officially recognised, and 10 January is a national Vodun holiday. Christianity and Islam are also widely practised, often alongside traditional beliefs.
French is the official language, and Fon and Yoruba are the most widely spoken of dozens of local languages.

culture.heading: Arts
paragraphs: Benin's royal art, including appliqué cloth and bronze work, is renowned. In 2021 France returned 26 treasures looted from Abomey in 1892. Musician Angélique Kidjo is internationally famous. Common foods include pâte (maize dough) with sauces and grilled fish.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: Benin is a presidential republic in which the president is head of state and government. After 1990 the country had peaceful changes of power, but electoral reforms since 2018 have excluded major opposition parties from some elections, drawing criticism.
Jihadist violence has spread from the Sahel into Benin's northern regions in recent years. In December 2025 an attempted coup was thwarted.

economy.heading: Cotton and the port
paragraphs: Agriculture employs a large share of the population, and Benin is one of Africa's largest cotton producers. Cashews and other crops are also exported. The Port of Cotonou is a key gateway for trade with Nigeria and landlocked Sahel countries, and informal re-export trade with Nigeria is significant.
Benin uses the West African CFA franc. Growth has been relatively strong, but poverty remains widespread.
